title: The transcriptomic era
objective: Explain how single-cell RNA sequencing redefined DRG neuron subtypes and what that enables.

steps.title: Letting the cells sort themselves
steps.body:
Instead of a few preset markers, **[[single-cell RNA sequencing]]** (A5 forward; C12 in depth) measures thousands of genes per neuron and groups cells by their whole expression profile.

Applied to DRG (first in 2015), this revealed on the order of a dozen or more molecularly distinct neuron types, more than the old bins.

steps.title: From catalog to control
steps.body:
An atlas is only a parts list. The payoff comes when each type gets a **genetic handle**, a Cre or Flp line, so you can label, record from, or manipulate it.

Recent toolkits (2024) provide exactly these handles for many DRG types, which is what makes subtype-specific DREADD experiments feasible.

flag.note: Cluster number and boundaries depend on method and analysis choices (C12).

steps.prompt: Order the modern workflow from discovery to manipulation.
items: Pick marker genes for a subtype of interest
Make or obtain a Cre/Flp line for those genes
Express a reporter or DREADD in that subtype
steps.explanation: Sequencing defines the parts; genetic lines turn a cluster on a plot into neurons you can actually switch on or off, the backbone of the colon paper and your project.

steps.prompt: A UMAP plot shows 12 DRG clusters. What can it tell you on its own?
options: That neurons differ in expression and fall into groups, but not their function, which needs genetic and physiological follow-up
steps.explanation: Clustering shows molecular groupings, not function, location or wiring. Those require the manipulations the rest of the curriculum teaches (C12 covers what UMAPs can and can't say).
